formulaCard.title: Cash Discount Amount
formulaCard.formula: $$\text{Cash Discount Amount} = \text{Net Price} \times \text{Cash Discount Rate}$$ $$\text{Amount Paid} = \text{Net Price} - \text{Cash Discount Amount}$$

explanation: A [[kw:cash discount]] is a reduction from the invoice (net) price given to encourage the buyer to pay before the credit period ends.
It is different from a trade discount: trade discounts are off the list price for retailers; cash discounts are off the net price for early payment.
Cash discounts are optional; the buyer chooses to pay early and take the discount, or pay the full amount later.
[[imp:Cash discounts are always calculated on the net merchandise price (after trade discounts), not including freight.]]
Common terms like 2/10, n/30 mean a 2% discount if paid within 10 days, otherwise the full net amount is due in 30 days.

hints: They might earn more by using the cash elsewhere.
Opportunity cost could be higher than 2%.

visuals.caption: Understanding the start date of the discount period is crucial.

formulaCard.formula: Ordinary: Discount ends = invoice date + discount days. Net due = invoice date + net days.
formulaCard.title: Determining Due Dates
notes: For EOM, add the days to the last day of the month.
For ROG, add days to the date goods were received.

explanation: Credit terms specify when payment is due and any discount for early payment.

[[kw:Ordinary dating]] (e.g., 2/10, n/30): discount period starts from the invoice date. 2/10 means 2% discount if paid within 10 days of invoice date. n/30 means the full (net) amount is due in 30 days.
[[kw:EOM dating]] (End Of Month): discount period starts after the end of the invoice month. Example: 2/10, n/30 EOM – if invoice dated July 8, the discount period runs until August 10.
[[kw:ROG dating]] (Receipt Of Goods): discount period starts when the buyer receives the goods, not the invoice date. Example: 2/10, n/30 ROG.
[[imp:Always identify the start date of the discount period before calculating the due date.]]

steps: Must pay by May 15 to get the 2% discount.
examples.title: A – Ordinary dating
examples.prompt: Invoice dated May 5, terms 2/10, n/30. What is the last day to take the cash discount?

steps: The discount period doesn't start until after the month ends.
So an invoice dated early in the month gets almost an extra month to pay.
For a July 2 invoice, discount doesn't start until August 1.
examples.title: B – EOM dating

examples.title: C – Find due date ROG
steps: ROG means discount period starts from receipt: June 18.
Must pay by June 28 to get discount.

discoveryHook.scenario: What if you can't pay the full invoice by the discount date, but you can pay part? Many sellers allow a cash discount on the portion paid, reducing the overall debt.

steps: The \$1,940 payment reduces the debt by \$2,000.
examples.prompt: Owe \$4,000, terms 3/10. Pay \$1,940 within 10 days. How much credit is received?
examples.title: A – Find credit from partial payment

examples.prompt: Explain the math: If the discount is 2%, why does dividing by 0.98 give the credit?
examples.peerPrompt: Think: the payment is 98% of the credit.
examples.title: B – Why does payment ÷ complement give the credit?
steps: If the credit (reduction) is C, then the cash paid is C – 2% of C = C × 0.98.
This tells us the full amount of debt that the partial payment covers after the discount.

examples.title: C – Outstanding balance
examples.prompt: Invoice \$6,000, terms 2/10. Buyer pays \$2,940 within 10 days. What is the remaining balance?

teacherCues: Explain that partial payments earn a cash discount only on the portion paid within the discount period.
Show how to calculate the outstanding balance.

visuals.caption: The cash discount effectively increases the payment's value toward the debt.
visuals.title: Partial Payment Calculation

explanation: Sometimes a buyer makes a partial payment within the discount period and wants to apply the cash discount to that portion.
To find how much credit is received for a partial payment: [[imp:Credit Received = Payment ÷ (1 – Cash Discount Rate).]]
The remaining balance after a partial payment is: [[imp:Outstanding Balance = Previous Balance – Credit Received.]]
Example: Owe \$2,000, pay \$980 within 2% discount period. Credit = \$980 ÷ 0.98 = \$1,000. New balance = \$2,000 – \$1,000 = \$1,000.

formulaCard.formula: $$\text{Credit Received} = \frac{\text{Partial Payment}}{1 - \text{Cash Discount Rate}}$$ $$\text{Outstanding Balance} = \text{Previous Balance} - \text{Credit Received}$$
notes: This applies only when payment is made within the discount period.
If payment is after the discount period, no discount applies.
formulaCard.title: Partial Payment Formulas

confusionCorner.title: Watch out!
confusionCorner.body: The partial payment benefit only applies during the discount period. [[imp:If payment arrives after the discount date, no discount is given.]]

confusionCorner.title: Watch out!
confusionCorner.body: Don't forget to add freight AFTER the cash discount is applied. [[imp:Freight is a separate charge and never receives a discount.]]

explanation: When an invoice includes trade discount, freight, and cash discount terms, follow this order:
1. Apply trade discount to list price to get net price.
2. Add freight (if FOB shipping point) to get total invoice amount.
3. If paying within discount period, apply cash discount to net price only.
4. For partial payments, compute credit on the portion paid within the discount period, then find the remaining balance.
[[imp:Always separate the merchandise portion from freight before calculating any cash discount.]]
